note.question: How should a platform schedule heterogeneous workers when fixed pay and assignment rules create different effective hourly wages and workers strategically choose when to be available?
note.overview: Under decentralized control (DC), workers strategically choose day-over-day availability and Equation (3) defines a Nash equilibrium; the paper restricts attention to markets where such an equilibrium exists. FCFS and PFCFS are allocation mechanisms: FCFS uses sequential advance slot reservation, whereas PFCFS elicits temporal types and is analyzed through incentive properties and worst-case performance guarantees.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Under DC, workers choose availability and the platform randomly allocates up to its myopic period cap; Equation (3) describes the resulting day-over-day availability equilibrium. Under FCFS, slots are released in advance and workers reserve them sequentially before becoming available. Under PFCFS, workers report temporal types and the mechanism bundles and prioritizes advance allocations before availability is realized. components.label: Day-over-day worker-availability Nash equilibrium under DC
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Day-over-day worker-availability Nash equilibrium under DC; mechanism outcomes under FCFS and PFCFS. Equation (3) on PDF p. 7 (printed p. 1774) defines mutual availability best responses only for decentralized control, and the paper restricts that analysis to instances where an equilibrium exists. FCFS is a sequential advance-reservation mechanism. Under PFCFS, truthful temporal-type reporting is weakly optimal but need not be the unique best report because a worker may report a superset of the true type without gaining utility; the mechanism is ex post individually rational.

source.quote: We capture the randomness in (a) driver types T (recall we sample the types using start-time and shift-length distributions) and (b) allocation policies themselves (recall all three allocation policies are ran­ domized) using 30 different seeds. (As it will become clear soon, because of the large number of drivers, the impact of the randomness on the output is relatively small.) Given the market parameters, the implementation of FCFS and PFCFS14 is straightforward (see the pseudo­ codes in Mechanisms 1 and 2, respectively) and the computation times were relatively low (less than a minute for a given market, that is, (c,a,muncon,T) tuple, on an Intel i7 3.8GHz 8-core processor with 16 GB 2667MHz DDR4 memory).
